review:
Gameplay wise, it has deviated a bit from the traditional Dawn Of War 2 campaigns in favour of a more Dawn Of War - Dark Crusade like meta campaign. You can now choose between Space Marines, Eldar, Orks, Chaos and the Imperial Guard. The campaigns are the same for everyone, however each race has their own agenda. But the goal of every race is to eliminate Azariah Kyras. That means even though the campaign feels redundant, it is refreshing to be able to change tactics and play the campaign as other races.

Retribution also brings some diversity to the campaigns, such that unlike the previous Dawn Of War 2 installments, you can now further diversify your forces by replacing your regular deployable hero units with other honor guard units, depending upon your play style or according to what sort of opposition you expect to face in the campaign. You can also now field a larger number of squads by capturing Relay Beacons (or equivalent for races other than the Space Marines) and call in additional squads or vehicles subject to the amount of Requisition you have captured during your battle. This makes your campaign similar to a skirmish game albeit with campaign like objectives.

You can also gain traits for your hero units faster since you get a guaranteed trait every time you level up, unlike previous Dawn Of War 2 installments, where you have to level up 2-3 times before you get a trait.

Though I feel its somewhat inferior to DOW2 and Chaos Rising story-wise, it is nonetheless interesting to see how the story ends for the Blood Ravens in the Space Marine campaign (which I believe is canon for this series).

As a developer, what would you do when your game is loved by a dedicated fanbase, but mired in dislike for it's stifling DRM? You make a stand alone expansion that is six times the original game and streamline it for an excellent online experience. Good guy Relic. 

Real Time Tactical Roleplaying Game. That is how I would describe Dawn of War Retribution. It is focussed on character building, and using special abilities to clear obstacles and objectives. Clearning these obstacles rewards you with gear and other sweet loot to use and to adapt to circumstances. However, unlike the original Dawn of War 2, this one does it with more than just the Space Marines. This time round the campaign is open to the zealous Space Marines, the dogmatic Imperial Guard,  the enigmatic Eldar, the barbaric Orks, the horrific Tyrranids and the eldritch Chaos Marines. Each faction proceeds through the same story and events, but does so for a different purpose. The Space Marines need to clear their name, as their chapter master allegedly has fallen to Chaos, while the Eldar pursue the same cause to prevent their planets from being destroyed by the Inquisition. The Orks just want to fight and the Tyrranids hunger. The voice acting in the game is top notch and delivers the ruminations of each character with gusto and panachel; Slightly over the top, yet in tune with the material. The overal experience is entertaining and diverse, allowing for many hours of gameplay on your own, or with a friend. 

The game also features and extensive multiplayer component to go head to head. It plays like your ordinary RTS, but allows for so much customisation in regards to outfits and paintjobs. You might be forgiven for thinking that Valve made this game. The overal experience is a fast paced stratagem, with more focus on skirmishes between parties than massive clashes between armies. 

The last mode, and perhaps the most entertaining is Last Stand. In this mode, you and two others try to fend off twenty waves of enemy hordes with customised hero units. The mode is amazing for its many options and rewarding gameplay. No matter how far you come, the game will always reward you with points or items for your effort. Get a friend to two and tackle this beast. You will be entertained.

I could go on to muse this game for another while, but if you're not really into the compact rts style, or Warhammer for that matter, then this game might not be your cup of tea. It can also get a bit boring after five campaigns. Especially the more human oriented races do feel a bit stale after a while. 

What? Of course not! Humans? Stale? Art thou mad? Humanity shall prevail. The Emperor wills it. The day that Chaos rules the minds of men shall never come. Stand fast fellow warrior and join us in the eternal battle against the foul beings that the vile warp hath unleashed. Forget you money; human lives are the Emperor's currency. So spend it well, and pay your debt to his Greatness!

Even after several years, this game still looks and plays well.  A shame they never got to release all of the armies, but it's still fun to go in and enjoy a game with friends.  Last Stand was a suprise hit that is remarkably entertaining for something so simple in its setup.  All in all, this game is definately worth your time and money.  Now integrated with Steamworks, there is renewed hope that Sega may bring the series back with more titles - fingers crossed !

Unfortunately, the Risk-style campaign map present in Dark Crusade does not exist in Retribution. Drawbacks aside, I'd recommend everyone to give it a try. It'll never accomplish what the original DoW did, but I think the series stands out for what it is: a fast-paced skirmish-oriented RTS game, based in the Warhammer 40K universe.

P.S. If you are looking for base-building and controlling huge armies, you won't find any of that here, the game focuses on taking key points around the map and getting the resources necessary to build a medium-sized force of some troops, a few elite units and a handful of vehicles, generally 3 to 5, for the most part.

Dawn of War 2 is a RTT, a Real Time Tactical game set in the Warhammer 40k universe. It closely resembles Company of Heroes  which is not surprising considering that the same people are responsible for both games. You start with a base (or Hive if you're playing as [url=https://vignette.wikia.nocookie.net/vsbattles/images/2/24/Tyranid.jpeg/revision/latest?cb=20160312120603] Tyranids [/url]  (a bug/reptile like alien species with ferocious appetite) and produce units to either destroy the enemy base (Conquest) or controlling certain areas of the map (Capture the Flag).

 It plays very differently to its predecessor because base building has been basically completely scrapped to focus more on the combat aspect. Units, which are grouped into squads,  are precious, because they gain experience while fighting which simply improves their stats. To do this, you have to use the cover mechanic in the game which makes your units tougher to kill. Flamethrowers and grenades will very fastly kill your units in bunkers though so you still have to take care of them. Also you can flee from disadvantageous battles to keep your squad alive to replenish it with units furthering the tactical aspect of the game.

The maps are symmetrical and pretty balanced from what I've seen and feature various climate zones within the galaxy. They play quite differently from each other so you can expect some variation here.

The playable factions in the game are the Empire which have on one side cheap cannon fodder and heavy tanks in the late game, the Space Marines which are basically what would happen if you would put the Crusades in a futuristic setting, Chaos which is basically the playable Hell faction with various demons and morbid creatures, the Tyranids which are some bug-like reptile creatures which will eat everything in their path, the Eldar which are basically Space Elves and the Orks which still don't know how to properly build a tank after millenia of war.

You can upgrade the units with certain weapons which require you to spend a certain amount of control point or energy, which are the two types of ressources this game has. Those can also be used to upgrade your base to unlock access to better units and even to some ultimate units which are still counterable by using the respective units.

The campaign in DOW2:Retribution is pretty poor in my opinion, because it's basically a rethread of the same thing over again with different factions. Once you played, you played them all. The Chaos Rising and base game campaign are way better in this regard, because their quality is vastly superior. If you want to play them though, you have to purchase the base game and the Chaos Rising expansion. By the way, the campaigns play very differently to the base game. It's more a story-driven RPG about various heroes from each faction. I didn't play the  campaigns to be honest but I know somebody who liked them a lot for their action-driven style.

There is also the Last Stand mode, my favourite game mode, in which you have a single hero fighting cooperatively with other players against waves of enemies trying to survive until wave 20, the last wave. Doing this, you level up your character which gets better gear over time until you reach level 20. Once there, you can reset your level to level 1 and get a prestige star. This procedure can be repeated 3 times. There is one hero for each faction of the game which plays very differently and if that's not enough you can purchase the Necron Overlord and Tau Commander DLC from two factions featured in the Warhammer 40k lore but not playable as RTT faction in the game. There are also some various purchasable gear which I would buy on sale even if it's actually good gear because it is pretty overpriced in my opinion. The other non-game DLCs are only worth it on sale.

TL;DR: RTT Experience in the Warhammer 40k with good campaigns and alternate game mode which is worth the price asked for.

This time you can choose rewards at the end which was nice, but early on it was frustrating to not get any of the wargear I actually wanted. It's also a little weird to have veterans lose their abilities from previous games and have to learn them all over again. At least Chaos Rising just increased the level cap; Retribution actually lowers it to 10.

So for single player, the game is totally worth it on sale. But for the full price? Eh, maybe wait for the sale.

DoW2 Retribution is a perfect blend of sqaud based combat with a variety of factions/races to enjoy playing, and is even better with the Elite Mod. Rather than having any base building and a deathball of units thrown at each time and time again, like starcraft and the original DoW, it introduces directional cover and other interesting mechanics.

- Cover: Grants damage mitigation and suppression resistance, getting to cover whenever you can is normally a good choice. 

- Suppression: Reduces a units movement and attack speed, units that are relatively close to the suppressed unit or targeted unit will also become suppressed, which is useful against large numbers melee infantry and ranged blobs.

- Unit Levelling: Units gain experience points as they battle which increases their health, damage and accuracy with their weapons. Max is lev4 for standard units and lev10 for the hero/commander.

- Wargear was an addition which allows for different counters and playstyles for each race. As such it plays a large role in modifying a unit for different battefield situations.
     - Flamer Weapons: Replaces and/or adds a flamer weapon which is good against light buildings, light infantry and units in cover.
     - Plasma Weapons: Very effective against heavy infantry.
     - Rocket Weapons: Inaccurate against all targets except vehicles and buildings.
     - Range of other weapons and wargear in-game
     - Heroes/Commanders have their own unique wargear, seperate from standard units, that can be assigned to them.

DOW2: Retribution is a disappointing step back from the previous Dawn of War 1 and even the base Dawn of War 2. [h1]Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II: Retribution is an excellent RTS-style game[/h1] where base-building itself is dropped, in favor of more strategic combat involvement. While this may seem initially like a dumbing-down from DoWI, the playstyle it encourages is more fast-paced, usually more aggressive, and leads itself to large armies splitting off across the map. This has ended up being a very fun way to play an RTS. 

[u]The campaign[/u] has benefited from this style in that in place of a Commander unit, you can have up to four Heroes that are powerful (typically single-person) units with Wargear upgrades and stat boosts while in a mission. These heroes can be substitued for an Honor Guard unit, which is a stronger version of a standard army unit. While building an army is fun, I also had a blast clearing the missions with only my Heroes and their witty banter.

[u]Multiplayer[/u] has become faster, which is usually a plus, as it allows us to play more games, or to boot up a match when normally we couldn't. I enjoy that gameplay feels more aggressive, with players capturing Requisition Points and Power Nodes in order to increase the speed that accumulate resources to purchase army units, and with holding the Victory Points, in which you must hold more than your opponent for a period of time in order to win. This leads to a very active playstyle, where you're balancing defensive capabilities with offensive, and mobility with firepower. Nearly every unit has potential upgrades, either as stat increases or new weapons, allowing them to be good against, and bad against, different types of enemies. Something as small as purchasing a few Flamers will make your unit that much stronger with melee engages, and constantly staying one step ahead of your enemy in upgrades, or creating units to counter their build, will often be the deciding factor of whether you fall from grace, or rise in glory as a successful tactician. The Hero system also carries into Multiplayer, as you select from one of six races, then one of three Hero units per race. These Heroes have different skills and Racial Abilities, and encourage different playstyles. Similar to the Campaign, these Hero units can purchase Wargear ingame once they have met the requirements (per game, no carrying over), to grant higher stats and capabilities against different enemies.

[u]The Last Stand[/u], also sold as an individual DLC package, is a great mode where three players try to survive, and conquer, 20 waves of enemies. Each player selects a Hero and their Wargear before entering queue, with seven different Heroes, and a LOT of Wargear options. Mirrors are possible, but do not generally affect gameplay, and will likely have different builds. Wargear is obtained through leveling up, where you gain experience points at the end of the game, or through special, sometimes difficult, achievements. Most Heroes have two achievement Wargear unlocks. The Last Stand is incredibly brutal, very unforgiving, and you may never beat it. Players have the ability to revive fallen teammates, though this immobilizes the reviver, and reduces their firepower greatly, easily causing their death as well. Also on the map are two Point Multiplying Nodes, similar in appearance to Power Nodes, that add a x3 multiplier to your team's score each. Certain types of enemies will try to capture these points for themselves. Each Hero is vastly different, and every team composition is as well, leading to immense replayability, especially if you haven't beaten either of the two maps yet... (It's always that blasted Wave 20! ;-;)

[u]Lore-wise this game is both engaging and genuinely gets the grimdark feel of the WH40k universe[/u]. As the story progressed, through the earlier two campaigns (DoWII and DoWII:Chaos Rising) and this one, I felt the tragedies come one after the other, and each victory feeling less and less impactful until you get that [i]one[/i] killing blow that just brings everything you've done all together, and you can feel the weight just disappear off of your chest, and you sit back in the chair and let out this sigh of relief... until you are informed of another emergency happening almost immediately. It kept me on the edge of my seat with its grimdarkness, its surprisingly fitting comedy (especially playing as those 'ard Ork boyz), and my genuine interest in how it was going to play out. While a lot of people feel that the campaign is short, and it kinda is, it certainly isn't lacking in content or gameplay, and it was very fun.

I know a lot of people weren't huge fans of the way the hero mechanic was used in this series, but being a long time RTS gamer myself, I enjoyed a break from the norm. Additionally, they've incorporated their own brand of survival mode called Last Stand, which is where I feel the entire DoW II series really shines. 

You choose and control a commander unit from one of the eight races, then match up with two other human players and play against wave after wave of increasingly difficult AI units. Each wave cleared provides experience, which is applied to your chosen commander and leads towards further war gear unlocks. Each level gained gives you access to more powerful abilities, attack types and survivability options.

The game has it's issues in executing some of what people have come to expect from the older games in the DoW series, but if you approach Retribution without these preconceived notions, you will find a lot to enjoy.

Ok, I normally can't be bothered to write a review, but there's a few things you should know before paying anything other than 75% off for this game. I'll keep it simple.

Single player campaign feels like a rushed afterthought. No more cool planetary backdrops or watching your ship jump into a new system. Now you get a static map and dumbed down levelling system. DoW II is better if you want single player, unless you simply HAVE to play as Orks/Eldar etc.

But wait! Multiplayer is what it's all about anyway right? It could be, but seeing as finding a public game that doesn't boot you out after the countdown reaches zero is next to impossible, you're limited to private matches. 

The Last Stand works fine, but if you only want to play that you can buy it seperately anyway.

Overall it's a shame, as DoW II is good fun, especially in multiplayer, but without the ability to actually play public matches, all Retribution really brings to the table is a new race to play as. On your own. If you want a solid multiplayer strategy game with an active community and servers that (mostly) work, get CoH instead.

Started the campaign with a simple objective:

Save the sector.

There are seven factions, multiple campaigns and enough enemies to make this feel less like a military operation and more like a personal disagreement with the entire galaxy.

The gameplay is still focused on squads rather than traditional base building.

Take cover.
Flank.
Use abilities.
Accidentally aggro half the map.

Then wonder why everyone is shooting at you.

The best part is watching your units become increasingly powerful throughout the campaign. At the beginning, every fight feels dangerous.

Later, your squad walks into a battlefield carrying enough explosives to solve most diplomatic issues permanently.

The campaign also gives you plenty of excuses to fight everyone.

Orks want to fight.

Chaos wants to corrupt everything.

Tyranids want to eat everything.

Eldar have a complicated plan that nobody understands.

The Imperium has paperwork.

Naturally, I chose violence.

Gameplay verdict: Excellent tactical RTS with satisfying squad progression, strong faction variety and fast combat. It sacrifices some of the base-building from the original Dawn of War II, but the focus on tactical abilities and squad management makes every battle feel more active.

It's especially satisfying when a carefully planned ability combo wipes out an entire enemy position.

It's less satisfying when the same thing happens to you.

10/10.

However, the game makes up for this with the best iteration of the wave survival mode, Last Stand.

Retribution is a stand-alone game and does not require DoW 2.
It is the end of the DoW 2 trilogy, ending the story of the Blood Ravens and giving us a somewhat complete package of all races (missing Necrons, Tau, Dark Eldar, Sororitas and Mechanicus but well..)

The game is the same as DoW2, so gameplay, music and everything else is on point.

You get a single campaign, which you can play through with different races. Not much changes but every race has it's own motivations and is voice acted.
Naturally completing it as Blood Ravens is the most canon one and the story will make sense.
But you can also play and experiment with builds as the Tyranids, Imperial Guard, Eldar, Orks or Chaos (yes Chaos vs Chaos, makes a lot of sense lol).


The Last Stand mode is improved and has 2 DLC commanders Tau and Necron.
(was their inclusion some kind of teaser for potentially playable races in DoW 4? sadly we will never know...)
